verses.note: Hebrews 11:4 says that by faith Abel offered a better sacrifice. The verse itself shows the outward difference, first and best against some; Hebrews locates the inward one, a heart that trusted God. The quality of the gift expresses the worshiper, which is why the text speaks of God regarding Abel and his offering, the person first.

Enoch's walk with God is set in the middle of ordinary life: it began after Methuselah's birth and continued while he had other sons and daughters. Hebrews 11:5-6 reads it as faith that pleased God, adding that without faith it is impossible to please him.
Hebrews 11:7 says Noah built the ark by faith, warned about things not yet seen, and in reverent fear. His faith is shown entirely in obedience carried out over a long time before any rain fell.

The command comes before any explanation of where or why. Abram is asked to act on God's word alone, which is why Hebrews 11:8 makes his departure a model of faith: he went out not knowing where he was going.
Faith here is simply walking where God has spoken. The man who has no child and no land sets out at seventy-five on the strength of a promise of both.

The same man who left everything at God's word now plans for survival as though God had promised nothing. Genesis records the lapse without softening it, and the pattern returns in 20:2 and with Isaac in 26:7. Faith in Scripture grows through failures like this one.
Abram can afford to let Lot choose because the land is already promised to him by God (12:7). Trust in God's promise frees him from the need to secure the best portion for himself.

Abram is told to walk through a land he does not own, among peoples who hold it, as though it were already his. Faith here means living on the ground of a promise before it is fulfilled, as Hebrews 11:9 describes.

Abram's refusal is faith in action. God had promised to bless him (12:2), and he will not let anyone else, least of all Sodom, take the credit. The next chapter answers him at once, with God promising to be his very great reward (15:1).
The Bible's first explicit statement of faith is trust in a person who has made a promise, not assent to an idea. Abram has nothing but God's word, and he rests on it.

Abraham must now carry a name that announces what he cannot see. Every time someone called him, the name repeated God's promise, and Paul makes this a picture of faith that believes God's word before the evidence (Romans 4:17-21).

Faith in Scripture is not the absence of honest astonishment. Abraham's laugh names exactly what makes the promise impossible, and Paul says he ‘faced the fact that his body was as good as dead’ and still did not waver (Romans 4:19-21).
Abraham has just laughed at the promise, yet he acts on it the same day. His obedience is the form his faith takes, which is the point James makes about Abraham (James 2:21-22).
Sarah laughed in doubt and now laughs in joy. Hebrews 11:11 still counts her among the faithful, which shows that Scripture measures faith by where it rests at last, not by whether it ever wavered.

A test in Scripture brings into the open what is already there. The verse assumes that faith is not only a belief held but a trust that can be tried, and that God may try it for the sake of the one who has it (Exodus 20:20, James 1:12).

Abraham's obedience is prompt and wordless. Hebrews 11:8 describes his first departure as going out without knowing where he was going, and this departure has the same shape: he goes toward a place he has not yet been shown.

Interpreters read "we will return" in different ways: as a father concealing the truth from his servants, as words said without knowing how they would come true, or as confidence that God would keep his promise through Isaac even beyond death. Hebrews 11:19 takes the third view, saying Abraham reasoned that God could raise the dead.

Abraham could have taken the land as a gift. He insists on paying so that no one can later question his title. Faith in God's promise does not make him careless in human dealings; it makes him scrupulous.

Her one-word answer commits her to a man she has never met in a land she has never seen, on the testimony of a servant about the God of Abraham. Rebekah's going echoes Abraham's own obedience to the call to go.

Genesis 15:6 says Abraham believed and it was counted to him as righteousness; this verse says he obeyed. James 2:21-23 reads the two together from Genesis 22: faith that is real acts, and Abraham's acts showed his faith complete.

Jacob has not yet called the LORD ‘my God’. The vow looks toward that confession, and 35:1-7 shows its fulfillment, when Jacob returns and builds an altar to the God who answered him in the day of his distress.
Faith here takes the form of argument from God's word against present danger. Jacob does not deny the threat; he sets God's promise against it.

Hosea reads this moment as prayer: Jacob "wept and sought His favor" (Hosea 12:4). The blessing is not seized by strength but asked for by one who can no longer fight, which is the posture of faith throughout Scripture.

Joseph's trust in God does not keep him from asking for human help. The Bible does not treat faith and ordinary requests as rivals: Paul, too, appealed to Caesar (Acts 25:11) while confessing that his life was in God's hands.

Jacob's unbelief is not defiance but the numbness of long grief. Scripture often shows faith struggling to accept good news that seems too good, as when the disciples disbelieved for joy at the risen Jesus (Luke 24:41).

Jacob's honesty about his hardships is part of what Hebrews finds admirable in the patriarchs: they "acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth" (Hebrews 11:13). Faith does not require calling a hard life easy.
Jacob's faith is shown in two acts: requiring a binding promise that he will be buried in the land, and then worshiping. He trusts a promise he will not see fulfilled in his lifetime.

The midwives act without any promise of protection. Their faith is shown as obedience to God against the most powerful authority they know, the pattern the apostles follow when they tell the council they must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29).
Hebrews 11:23 counts this hiding as an act of faith: Moses' parents were not afraid of the king's edict. The verse shows faith working in a small, hidden act of protection long before any miracle.

Hebrews 11:27 says that by faith Moses left Egypt, not fearing the king's anger, while verse 14 here says Moses was afraid. Interpreters resolve this in two main ways: some take Hebrews to refer to the exodus itself, when Moses left without fear; others think Hebrews refers to this flight and sees Moses' departure, whatever his fear of arrest, as a choice of God's people over Egypt.

The chapter's first verse raises the question its last verse answers: will they believe? Faith is presented here as trust in a messenger's report that God has appeared, the same structure the New Testament gives to faith in the apostles' witness to Christ (Romans 10:14-17).

The people's faith is a response to God's word and the signs that confirm it, and it leads directly to worship. The next chapter will test it hard, and by 6:9 the people cannot listen because of their broken spirit. The pattern of faith given, tested, and renewed runs through the rest of the book (14:31).

Israel eats a meal of departure while still under Pharaoh's roof. Dressing for the road before the release has happened is itself an act of trust in God's word, which is how Hebrews 11:28 reads Moses' keeping of the Passover.
The Israelites obey a command whose promise has not yet been fulfilled. Their obedience is the form their trust takes, which is why Hebrews can describe the Passover as kept by faith.
To test God is to make trust conditional on proof. The verse treats that as rebellion, not honest questioning, because it sets the terms God must meet.
Bold prayer grows out of God's prior word. David's confidence is not in his standing but in what God has said, which is the pattern of faith throughout Scripture.
The psalm's final word is not threat but invitation. The same rulers who plotted against the Anointed are offered refuge in him, and the beatitude reaches ‘all’.
The prayer is grounded not in the psalmist's merit but in where he has put his trust. Taking refuge in God is the Psalter's basic description of faith.
Trust draws on the memory of God's past faithfulness to his people. Paul uses the same language of hope that is not put to shame (Romans 5:5; 10:11).

Before any command, Isaiah names the fear. The first word of faith in this chapter is not a doctrine but a posture, quietness before a threat that looks larger than it is. Isaiah will state the same principle in 30:15: in quietness and trust is your strength.

Faith in this verse is not an opinion but a place to stand. The same root gives amen and emunah, faithfulness. Isaiah calls the king to lean his weight on God's promise to David (2 Samuel 7:16, whose promise that David's house will endure uses the same Niphal verb, neeman), and warns that there is no other footing.

Strength is exchanged, not generated. The verse describes faith as dependence: those who wait on God receive his strength because they have stopped relying on their own, which even the young cannot sustain.

The song opens with unbelief, not faith. What God did in his Servant was so unlike what anyone expected that no one believed the report. Faith, when it comes in this chapter, is the confession of people who had been wrong.

Ezekiel's answer is a model of faith that does not presume. He does not say the bones will live, since nothing he sees suggests it; nor does he say they cannot, since God is asking. Faith here is trust placed in God's knowledge where human sight fails.
God's future for his people includes taking away what they relied on in place of him. Micah treats military power as a rival object of trust, the point of Psalm 20:7 and Hosea 14:3.

The leaders' confession is that the city's strength lies in its God. Military success is credited not to Judah's fighters or Jerusalem's walls but to the LORD of Hosts, the point of the whole chapter.

The New Testament remembers Rahab for faith (Hebrews 11:31) and for acting on it (James 2:25), and Ruth's vow to take Naomi's God as her own (Ruth 1:16) is the Old Testament's classic confession of a convert. Both women entered the people of God by trust, not by birth.

Joseph believes the message and acts on it at once, at the cost of whatever the neighbors would think. Matthew's first picture of faith is not a confession but an obedient deed, which fits the Gospel's insistence on doing the Father's will (7:21).

Faith takes God at his word without staging tests to make him prove it. Jesus will be kept by his Father, but through the cross and the resurrection, not by being spared a fall; the same refusal returns when he is challenged to come down from the cross (27:40-43).
Worry is traced to little faith, not to lack of information. The remedy Jesus offers is not reassurance about outcomes but a truer view of the Father.
Genuine faith is recognized by its fruit. James makes the same argument when he says faith without works is dead (James 2:17-18).
Confession of Jesus as Lord is essential (Romans 10:9), but a confession that never becomes obedience is empty. The verse joins what the lips say to what the life does.

The centurion's faith is trust in the power of Jesus' spoken word, without sight, touch, or presence. Matthew sets it at the head of the chapter's teaching on faith, and it is the pattern for readers who will never see Jesus in the flesh (compare John 20:29).

Faith here is not membership but response. Jesus measures it and finds the largest example in someone with no covenant standing, which prepares for the chapter's warning that belonging to the kingdom is not inherited.

The disciples have enough faith to wake Jesus and pray to him, and not enough to be unafraid while he sleeps. Oligopistia names that condition. Jesus rebukes it and then saves them anyway, so the verse teaches both that fear in his presence is a failure of faith and that his help does not wait for great faith.

The faith Jesus sees belongs to the carriers as well as the man. The verse gives a place to faith exercised on another's behalf, which is part of why the church has read it in connection with intercessory prayer.
The father believes that Jesus' touch can restore a life already ended. His faith asks more than any request so far in these chapters, and Jesus goes with him without a word of testing.
Jesus credits her faith, not the cloth. Her faith was imperfect in its understanding, perhaps close to magic, but it reached for Jesus, and he honored it and corrected nothing but her hiding.

Jesus draws out an explicit confession before he heals. The faith he asks for is not confidence in a result but trust in him, ‘that I am able’, and the healing is given ‘according to’ that trust, not as a reward for its size.
The greatest of the prophets brings his uncertainty straight to Jesus. The verse gives the church a model for honest doubt: not silence or departure, but a question addressed to the one it concerns.
Faith here is the refusal to stumble over Jesus as he actually is. The blessing belongs not to those who never question but to those who keep trusting him when he does not match their expectations.

Jesus does not refuse evidence; he has just healed a blind and mute man. He refuses a sign on demand, which would put God under the demanders' control. Faith responds to what God gives, and the sign he gives is the death and resurrection of his Son.

Matthew's wording does not make Jesus' power dependent on faith; he ‘did not’ do many miracles, not that he could not. Unbelief closes people to what Jesus gives, and Matthew consistently links his mighty works to people who come in trust (8:10, 9:22, 9:29, 15:28).

Peter's faith acts on a word of command, not on a feeling of confidence. He asks for Jesus' order, receives it, and steps out. The verse defines faith by its object: Peter walks on the water not because he is strong but because Jesus has said, ‘Come’.

Jesus calls Peter ‘little faith’, not ‘no faith’: the faith that got him out of the boat was real, but his attention moved from the word to the wind. Doubt here is a divided mind in a believer, and Jesus meets it with a hand before a question. The same verb for doubt returns in 28:17, where some of the disciples doubt even as they worship the risen Jesus, and he comes near to them.

Her faith accepts the order Jesus states without resentment and argues from it: if Israel's Messiah has bread for his children, there is enough to spare for her. Luther's sermon on the text (1525) described her as taking Jesus at his own word. Faith here is humble, persistent, and theologically sharp all at once.

Jesus calls no one else's faith great in Matthew, though he marveled at the Gentile centurion's (8:10). Both are Gentiles, both ask for someone else, both are healed at a distance. The verse shows that faith, not ancestry, is what receives the Messiah's mercy, and it answers the chapter's opening question about clean and unclean.

Little faith in Matthew is not unbelief but trust that shrinks before a present need. Jesus treats memory as the remedy: faith grows by recalling what he has already done, which is why the questions recite the loaves, the crowds, and the baskets.

Unbelief here is the condition of a generation, and the disciples are not exempt from it. Yet Jesus' exasperation ends in a command that brings the boy to him: his patience with faithless people is itself part of what he bears.

Jesus measures faith not by its quantity but by whether it is truly trust in God. Tiny faith is enough because God does the moving. The verse therefore cannot be used to blame the sick for their illness or to promise results to those who believe hard enough; its reproof is aimed at disciples who had drifted into treating authority as their own.

Leaving everything to follow Jesus is faith in action, the opposite of the young man's choice. Peter's question shows that genuine faith can still carry a merchant's arithmetic, which Jesus does not scold but reshapes.

The promise rests on faith in God, not in faith itself. Matthew's Jesus teaches boldness in prayer (7:7-11, 18:19) and also prays in Gethsemane that the Father's will be done (26:39), so the verse encourages undivided trust rather than a technique for getting what one wants.

The refusal makes a point about the person's own relation to the bridegroom: no one can be ready on another's behalf. Readers from Augustine onward have taken the oil to stand for something inward (love, a good conscience, faith that works), precisely because it cannot be passed from one lamp to another.
The object of faith is the gospel, the announcement of what God is doing. Faith in Mark is trust in God's action in Jesus, which later scenes show can be small and yet real (9:24).
The man's faith is real but incomplete: he believes Jesus can, and wonders whether he will. Jesus answers the question he did not quite ask.
The faith Jesus sees belongs to the friends as well as the man. The verse gives a picture of faith that carries another person to Jesus when he cannot come himself.

Faith in the sense this parable teaches is a hearing that welcomes and keeps bearing fruit. The differing yields suggest that fruitfulness is not uniform, and the verse makes no ranking of believers by it.

Faith here is trust in Jesus' care and presence in danger, not confidence that no danger will come. Fear and faith are set against each other, and the question oupō, ‘not yet’, implies that faith is expected to grow from what the disciples have already seen.

Her faith is mixed with what looks like superstition, and it is secret. Jesus neither mocks it nor lets it stay as it is: he will call it faith and then bring her face to face with him. The verses show that faith can be real before it is well understood.
Jesus credits her faith, not the cloak. Faith is not a power that heals but trust that reaches for Jesus, and by drawing her forward he turns a touch of his clothes into a meeting with him.

Faith is asked for exactly when circumstances make it seem pointless. Jesus sets fear and faith against each other again, as after the storm (4:40), and asks Jairus to keep trusting past the report of death.

Mark uses the word apistia, unbelief, for the first time here. The verse links Jesus' mighty works with faith in those who receive them (compare 5:34, 9:23-24): not because faith is a force that makes miracles happen, but because Jesus' works are personal acts of rescue offered to those who come to him.

Mark is candid that even the disciples, who have seen the feeding with their own eyes, can have hardened hearts. Faith is not the automatic result of seeing miracles; it requires understanding who Jesus is, which Mark presents as a gift the disciples have not yet fully received (8:17-21).

Her faith is a humble persistence that takes Jesus' word seriously and still expects mercy from it. She does not claim a right to the bread; she trusts that there is enough of it to reach her. That combination of humility and bold expectation is what Jesus rewards.

Jesus' power works across distance and across the border between Jew and Gentile. Like the centurion's servant in Matthew 8:5-13, another Gentile healed at a distance, the healing depends on trusting his word rather than being near him.

The disciples have seen both feedings and still fret about bread. Their failure shows that faith is not produced by exposure to miracles; understanding who Jesus is requires a sight he gives, as the two-stage healing that follows will picture.

Faith in Mark is a sight Jesus gives, and it can come in stages. The man was not less healed for needing two touches; the disciples, who see Jesus as Messiah but not yet as the crucified one, are in the middle of the same healing.
Unbelief here is a condition of a whole generation, not only of outsiders. The disciples, who had cast out demons before, are included in it; faith is not a possession secured by past success.

The father's prayer shows that faith and doubt can coexist in one person, and that faith includes asking for more faith. Jesus heals in response to this mixed confession, which the church has long held up as a pattern for honest prayer.

Faith here is persistent, personal trust in Jesus as the one who can give sight. It is credited as the channel of the healing, not its power, and it issues in following. Bartimaeus is Mark's picture of the disciple the Twelve were meant to be.

Faith is directed at God, not at the strength of one's own believing. The saying teaches that nothing God wills is too large for prayer, and in context it tells disciples that God's purposes do not depend on the temple that is about to fall.

The first proclamation of the risen Jesus is met with disbelief by his closest followers. The passage makes no attempt to present the apostles as credulous; faith in the resurrection came to them against their expectation and through testimony they at first rejected.

Luke writes so that a believer who has already been taught can know the ‘certainty’ of it. Faith here is not opposed to evidence; it is instruction strengthened by an orderly account of what happened.
Zechariah is righteous (verse 6) and still doubts. Luke shows that faith is not a fixed possession of the devout; a lifelong priest can falter at the very promise he prayed for.
Unbelief does not stop God's word; it only keeps the doubter from speaking about it. The discipline is also mercy: Zechariah's silence ends in praise (1:64).
Mary's troubled reasoning is not unbelief. Luke shows a faith that thinks, questions, and then consents, in contrast with the demand for proof in verse 18.
Mary's question seeks understanding and is not rebuked. Scripture distinguishes the honest question of faith from the demand for a sign (compare verse 18).
Mary's faith is expressed as availability: she places herself under God's word before she knows what it will cost. Elizabeth will pronounce the blessing on this faith in verse 45.
The first beatitude in Luke is spoken over belief in God's word. Its contrast with Zechariah's silence is deliberate.
Zechariah's first act after months of silence is obedience to the angel's word. The man who doubted now confirms the promise in writing before his speech returns.
The shepherds act on what the Lord ‘has made known’ before they see anything. Faith in Luke is a response to God's word that goes and looks.
Faith trusts God's promises without staging tests to make him prove them. Jesus will be protected by God in the end, but by resurrection, not by being spared from falling.
Simon's faith at this stage is thin but real: he doubts the plan and obeys the person. Luke shows faith beginning as obedience to Jesus' word before it understands.
Faith here belongs to a group and shows itself in costly effort. Jesus responds to it on behalf of the man, which shows that the faith of others can bring a person to where grace is given.

The centurion's faith is joined to humility. He does not argue from his gifts, as his friends did, but from his lack of standing, and he asks for mercy on that basis. Luke's portrait of faith here is a person who expects everything from Jesus and claims nothing for himself.

Jesus measures faith by its object and its trust, not by its holder's lineage or merit. The first person in Luke's Gospel whose faith Jesus praises outright is a Gentile who has not even seen him, which anticipates the church of Acts, where people believe through the word of messengers.

Faith is not only belief that Jesus can act but trust in the way he chooses to act. The beatitude blesses those who keep trusting when Jesus is not the Messiah they pictured, which is the test John faces in prison and the church faces often.

Jesus credits her salvation to her faith, not to her tears or her gift. The actions in the scene are faith made visible, the trust that brought her into a Pharisee's house to seek him, and Luke uses the same saying for others who come to Jesus in need (8:48, 17:19, 18:42).

Faith here is not the absence of fear but trust in the one who is present in the boat. The disciples' cry was to Jesus, which is faith of a kind; his question asks them to trust him while he sleeps, not only when he wakes.

Her faith was imperfect in form, a secret touch in a crowd, yet Jesus names it as the means of her healing. He does not let it remain secret, because faith in Luke is finally a relationship with him, not a private transaction with his power.

The call to believe comes after the news of death, when faith no longer has any reason in circumstances. Luke places the woman's healing between the father's request and the report of death so that her story becomes the ground of Jesus' word to Jairus.

The promise is addressed to those who trust the Father enough to keep asking. Faith here is not a technique but the confidence that God hears, which is why the verse begins with ask rather than with any condition.

Hearing and keeping belong together. Luke's Mary is the model, blessed because she believed (1:45), which is why Christian traditions that differ on her place agree that her greatness lies in her faith.
Faith is not only private trust but public confession. Paul joins the two when he says that one believes with the heart and confesses with the mouth (Romans 10:9-10).
Anxiety about clothing is called little faith: not no faith, but faith that has not yet reckoned with the Father's care. Jesus' rebuke is an invitation to trust more, not a condemnation.

The command does not make entry a reward for effort, since the door belongs to the master who opens and shuts it. It makes response urgent: faith that enters now, rather than intends to later, is what the verse calls for, and Paul uses the same verb of the effort that grace produces (Colossians 1:29).

Jesus shifts the question from how much faith to what faith rests on. The smallest faith is enough because its power lies in God. The saying stands against any teaching that treats faith as a force the believer must build up to obtain results.
The faith Jesus commends is not only trust that obeyed on the road but trust that returned to him. The verse shows faith as a relationship with the healer, not simply a means to a cure.
Faith here is endurance: continuing to cry to God when his answer seems slow. The verse leaves the question open for each hearer, which is why the chapter goes on to show who in fact has faith.

The man's faith is shown in his persistence and his confession of Jesus as Son of David and Lord. Jesus names that faith as the channel of his healing and salvation, which answers the question of verse 8: here, at least, the Son of Man finds faith on the earth.

Peter had confessed Jesus as ‘the Christ of God’ (9:20). Now he cannot admit he knows him to a servant girl. The verse shows that faith in Luke is not a single confession but a loyalty that can be lost in a moment of fear, and Jesus' prayer in verse 32 is what holds it.
His faith has no evidence to lean on but the manner of Jesus' dying and a few words of prayer. The request is simple and personal, ‘remember me’, and it is enough.

The apostles did not believe easily. Their faith in the resurrection came against their expectations and after they had rejected the first report, which is part of why Luke can present them as witnesses rather than as people who believed what they wished.

Receiving Christ and believing in his name are the same act described twice. Faith in John is not assent to a list but welcome of a person, the one whose name, meaning his identity, has just been revealed.
Faith in John begins with hearing a witness and acting on it. The two disciples have seen no sign yet; they follow on the strength of testimony, the way the Gospel's readers are meant to (20:29-31).
Jesus neither rejects faith based on a sign nor treats it as complete. In John, faith grows through seeing more of who Jesus is, from the first signs to the cross and resurrection.

Mary's instruction is a model of trust that does not dictate. Catholic and Orthodox readers have seen in it Mary's role of directing others to her Son, and Protestant readers a pattern of faith for every disciple; the two readings are not exclusive, and both rest on the words themselves: do whatever he tells you.

The disciples already believed in some sense (1:41-49), and yet ‘his disciples believed in him’ after the sign. In John faith is not a single moment but a trust that deepens as Jesus reveals himself, as verse 22 will show again.

The same verb names both sides: many believed, but Jesus did not believe himself to them. Faith drawn by spectacle is real but not yet the trust that Jesus answers with self-giving; the chapter shows the difference without despising the beginning.

Nicodemus believes something true about Jesus on the basis of signs, and Jesus does not dismiss it. The chapter shows that faith resting on signs is a beginning, not yet the new birth that sees the kingdom.
In Numbers, whoever looked at the snake lived. Faith is compared to that look: not an achievement, but turning toward what God has provided.
Believing Jesus is described as endorsing God's truthfulness. The reverse is drawn in 1 John 5:10: whoever does not believe God has made him a liar.

Faith and obedience are paired: believing the Son and refusing him are the only two options the verse allows. Faith is not a private opinion but submission to the Son whom the Father has placed over all things.
The Samaritans move from believing because of a witness to believing because of Jesus' own word. Testimony brings people to Jesus; faith that lasts rests on hearing him.
The father's faith passes from wanting Jesus present to trusting his word in his absence. John's readers, who would never see Jesus, are shown that his word is enough (20:29).
Jesus locates unbelief in what people love. The desire for human approval makes faith impossible because faith means receiving honor from God alone, which may cost honor among people (12:42-43).

A crowd that follows because of signs is where the chapter starts, not where it ends. John has already shown that belief resting on signs alone is not yet the trust Jesus looks for (2:23-25), and this chapter will sift such a crowd down to the few who stay for his words.

Jesus distinguishes seeking him for his gifts from seeing what his gifts reveal. Faith in John is not a response to having one's needs met but a recognition of who meets them; a crowd can be fed and followed and still not believe.

Jesus reduces all the works of God to one: believing in the Son. Faith is not one work among many that earns life; it is the reception of the one God sent. Christians who debate how faith and works relate agree that this verse puts faith at the center and directs it to a person, not a program.

The verse defines faith by its object and its effect. To believe is to come to Jesus himself, and what faith receives is not a benefit apart from him but his own life, which satisfies as bread satisfies the hungry.

Peter's faith does not rest on having understood the hard saying. It rests on who Jesus is and on the life his words give. Faith here is staying when others leave, because there is nowhere else to find life.

The brothers know Jesus' works and still do not believe. John shows that nearness and familiarity do not produce faith; the same brothers appear among the believers after the resurrection (Acts 1:14), so unbelief here is not the end of their story.

Some believe because of the signs, and John counts it as belief. The chapter also shows how quickly such belief can divide and waver (7:43), which is why the Gospel keeps pointing from the signs to the one they signify (20:30-31).
The man's faith begins as bare testimony: this is what happened to me. John shows faith growing from what one knows toward whom one knows, and the man's first title for Jesus is only the beginning.

The man's witness is limited but unshakable. He does not claim more than he knows, and he will not say less. John presents this as the seed of faith: testimony to what Jesus has done, which opens the way to knowing who he is (verses 35-38).

The Baptist's testimony bears fruit after his death. Faith here rests not on a new sign but on the recognition that the witness was true, which is how John's Gospel hopes its own readers will believe (19:35, 20:31).

Jesus values the disciples' faith more than their comfort, and even more than preventing a friend's death. The verse shows that faith is the aim of the signs, which is the stated aim of the whole Gospel (20:31).
Faith here is the condition for seeing what God is doing, not the power that makes it happen. Martha's objection does not stop the sign; Jesus asks her to trust him past what her senses tell her.
Believing in the light is presented as time-sensitive: the opportunity is real but not endless. The verse joins the Gospel's many invitations with a warning that refusing the light has consequences.
Faith that refuses to confess is presented as incomplete, because it still seeks approval from people rather than from God (5:44). The New Testament joins believing and confessing (Romans 10:9-10).

The remedy Jesus offers for fear is not information about the future but trust, and trust with a double object: God and Jesus together. The verse assumes what the Gospel argues from its first line (1:1), that faith in Jesus is not a second faith beside faith in God but the same faith.
Jesus does not despise faith that needs reasons. He invites the disciples to trust his word, and failing that to consider his works, the same appeal he made to his opponents in 10:37-38.

If unbelief is the root sin, faith is not one virtue among many but the turning of the whole person to God's Son. The verse makes believing in Jesus the dividing line on which the Spirit's conviction turns.

The disciples' confession is right in content: Jesus did come from God. What they lack is not the right words but the strength that comes only after the cross and the Spirit. The Gospel treats their faith as real but immature, and does not despise it.

Joseph's faith had been real but hidden. The death of Jesus, which scattered the open disciples, brings the secret one into the open. John does not scorn his earlier fear; he shows faith growing courage when it matters most.

The first Easter faith in John comes from seeing the evidence of the empty tomb, before the risen Lord appears and before Scripture is understood. Faith here is a response to what God has done, and understanding of Scripture follows (2:22, 12:16).

Jesus does not despise Thomas's faith, but he pronounces a blessing on faith that rests on testimony rather than sight. That is the faith the Gospel is written to create (verse 31), and it is not second-class: 1 Peter 1:8 speaks of believers who love him without having seen him and rejoice with inexpressible joy.

The Gospel states its own purpose: faith in Jesus as Messiah and Son of God, leading to life. Everything in it, signs, discourses, passion, and resurrection, was selected for that end. Believing here is not only assent to a proposition but the trust through which life is received ‘in his name’, that is, through his person and authority.

By joining obedience and faith in one phrase, Paul shows that the faith he preaches is not bare assent. Faith submits to the one it trusts, which is why the letter can teach justification by faith apart from works and still end in chapters 12-15 with a whole life reshaped.

The righteousness God reveals is received on the basis of faith and for faith. Faith here is not a contribution that earns; it is the posture of the one who lives by God's faithfulness, as Habakkuk's righteous man waited on God's vision.

On either reading of the genitive, righteousness reaches people by faith: the phrase ‘to all who believe’ makes human trust the means of receiving it. The subjective reading adds that the ground is Christ's own faithful obedience, a thought Paul states outright in 5:19.

Faith excludes boasting because it receives rather than achieves. What boasting is excluded is debated: boasting in ethnic privilege (the New Perspective's emphasis) or boasting in one's own obedience. Simon Gathercole (Where Is Boasting?, 2002) argued that Jewish boasting included confidence in obedience as the ground of final vindication, and that 4:2-5 shows Paul has both in view.

Abraham's faith was trust in God's promise when there was nothing to see. What was credited to him was not his achievement but his reliance on God's word, which is why Paul can make him the model for every believer.
Abraham's fatherhood extends to all who believe, Gentiles included. Faith, not ethnicity or ritual, is the family resemblance of Abraham's children.

Faith in Romans 4 is not denial of reality but trust in God in the face of it. Abraham took full account of his body and Sarah's womb and still relied on God's power, which is faith of a different kind from wishful thinking.

Faith glorifies God by taking him at his word. The contrast with 1:18-32 is deliberate: where humanity refused God glory and exchanged the Creator for creatures, Abraham gave glory to the God who creates and raises the dead.

Christian faith has the same object as Abraham's: the God who gives life to the dead. Abraham believed God would bring life from dead bodies; believers trust the God who has done that in raising Jesus.
The first act of Christian obedience here is an act of faith: to count as true what God says is true. The command comes before any effort, and it governs every effort that follows.

‘Children of the promise’ links this chapter to Romans 4 and Galatians 4, where Abraham's true children are those who share his faith in God's promise. Belonging to God's people rests on God's word received, not on birth.

The failure Paul identifies is not a lack of zeal (10:2 grants that Israel is zealous for God) but a wrong way of pursuit. Faith receives what works cannot earn. The debate over whether ‘works’ means any human effort (the Reformation reading) or the law's boundary markers of Jewish identity (the New Perspective on Paul, associated with James Dunn and N. T. Wright) continues here as in Galatians.

Faith in the stone God has laid is the dividing line. Those who trust him will not be put to shame; those who reject him stumble over him. Paul will repeat the promise in 10:11 with ‘everyone’, extending it to Jew and Gentile alike.
Paul does not value faith as a sincere attitude apart from its object. If what faith trusts did not happen, the faith is empty however deeply held. Christian faith is trust in an event.

Whatever the phrase pistis Christou means, the verse says plainly that Paul and Peter ‘believed in Christ Jesus’. Faith is trust directed to a person, and it is the way even the most privileged enter right standing with God.
Faith comes by hearing. The Spirit was not a reward for religious achievement but the gift that came with believing the message about the crucified Christ.

The verse makes grace the source, faith the channel, and God the giver. Whether faith is itself named as the gift here or included within the larger gift, the verse leaves nothing in salvation that originates in the person saved.
Jesus himself trusts God. Hebrews will later call him the pioneer and perfecter of faith (12:2): the life of faith is not only asked of believers but lived by their leader.
Unbelief is not treated as an intellectual doubt but as a condition of the heart that turns away from a living person. Faith, correspondingly, is continuing trust in the living God.
Faith that began must be held to the end. The verse ties sharing in Christ to faith that lasts, whatever tradition one follows in explaining how the condition relates to God's keeping.
Entrance into God's rest is by faith, and unbelief shuts people out. In Hebrews, unbelief and disobedience are two names for one refusal to trust God's word.
The gospel profits only when it is received with faith. The same good news that saves one hearer leaves another unchanged, and the difference is trust.
Faith and patience together inherit the promises. The pairing anticipates chapter 11, where faith is shown by people who waited, often without seeing the promise fulfilled.
Faith here is the confidence with which a cleansed person draws near to God. Its ‘full assurance’ rests on the priest and the cleansing just described, not on the worshiper's feelings.

Hebrews uses Habakkuk 2:4 differently from Paul. Paul stresses faith as the way one is counted righteous (Romans 1:17); Hebrews stresses faith as the way the righteous keep living, enduring until the promise comes. The two uses are complementary, and chapter 11 will illustrate the second.
Faith is defined by its opposite: not shrinking back. It is the persevering trust that keeps going toward the promise, and it is the subject of the whole next chapter.

The call to faith here is a call to accept captivity or death without retaliation, trusting that God will judge. Faith in Revelation is loyalty that holds under pressure, the same pairing of endurance and faith that 14:12 repeats.
